questions.question: If the sum of the diagonal elements of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix is \(-6\), then the maximum possible value of determinant of the matrix is ________.
questions.explanation: Let \(x\) and \(y\) be the two eigenvalues of the given \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(A\). We know from the fundamental properties of matrices that the sum of the eigenvalues is equal to the trace (sum of diagonal elements) of the matrix: \[\text{Trace}(A) = x + y = -6 \implies y = -6 - x \qquad \text{--- (1)}\] Similarly, the determinant of a matrix is equal to the product of its eigenvalues: \[|A| = x \cdot y\] \[|A| = x(-6 - x) = -6x - x^2\] Let this be represented as a continuous single-variable function \(f(x)\): \[f(x) = -6x - x^2\] \[f'(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left(-6x - x^2\right) = -6 - 2x\] \[-6 - 2x = 0 \implies x = -3\] \[f''(x) = \frac{d}{dx}(-6 - 2x) = -2\] Since \(f''(-3) = -2 < 0\), the function achieves a local maximum at \(x = -3\). Substituting \(x = -3\) back into our function to compute the maximum determinant: \[\text{Maximum Determinant} = f(-3) = -6(-3) - (-3)^2 = 18 - 9 = \boxed{9}\]

questions.question: The maximum value of ``\(a\)'' such that the matrix \[\begin{pmatrix} -3 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & a & -2 \end{pmatrix}\] has three linearly independent real eigenvectors is
questions.explanation:
\[|A - \lambda I| = 0\] \[\begin{vmatrix} -3 - \lambda & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 - \lambda & 0 \\ 0 & a & -2 - \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\] \[(-3 - \lambda) \left[(-1 - \lambda)(-2 - \lambda) - 0\right] - 0 - 2 \left[1(a) - 0\right] = 0\] \[(-3 - \lambda)(-1 - \lambda)(-2 - \lambda) - 2a = 0\] \[a = -\frac{1}{2}(3 + \lambda)(1 + \lambda)(2 + \lambda)\] \[a = -\frac{1}{2}\left(\lambda^3 + 6\lambda^2 + 11\lambda + 6\right)\] \[\frac{da}{d\lambda} = -\frac{1}{2}\left(3\lambda^2 + 12\lambda + 11\right) = 0\] \[3\lambda^2 + 12\lambda + 11 = 0\] \[\lambda = \frac{-12 \pm \sqrt{(12)^2 - 4(3)(11)}}{2 \times 3} = \frac{-12 \pm \sqrt{144 - 132}}{6}\] \[\lambda = \frac{-12 \pm \sqrt{12}}{6} = \frac{-12 \pm 2\sqrt{3}}{6} = -2 \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\] To distinguish between local maximum and minimum values, we compute the second derivative test: \[\frac{d^2a}{d\lambda^2} = \frac{d}{d\lambda}\left[-\frac{1}{2}\left(3\lambda^2 + 12\lambda + 11\right)\right] = -\frac{1}{2}(6\lambda + 12) = -3\lambda - 6\]
  • At \(\lambda = -2 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\): \[\frac{d^2a}{d\lambda^2} = -3\left(-2 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) - 6 = 6 - \frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} - 6 = -\frac{6}{2\sqrt{3}} = -\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} < 0 \quad \implies \text{(Local Maximum)}\]
  • At \(\lambda = -2 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\): \[\frac{d^2a}{d\lambda^2} = -3\left(-2 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) - 6 = 6 + \frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} - 6 = \frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} > 0 \quad \implies \text{(Local Minimum)}\]
Thus, the maximum value occurs at \(\lambda = -2 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). Substituting this value back into the function of \(a\): \[a_{\text{max}} = -\frac{1}{2}\left(3 + \left(-2 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\right)\left(1 + \left(-2 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\right)\left(2 + \left(-2 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\right)\] \[a_{\text{max}} = -\frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(-1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\] \[a_{\text{max}} = -\frac{1}{2}\left(\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2 - (1)^2\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = -\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{3} - 1\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\] \[a_{\text{max}} = -\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = \frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\] \[\boxed{\text{(B) $\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$}}\]
Key points
  • Characteristic Expansion: For an \(n \times n\) matrix, the characteristic equation yields an \(n^{\text{th}}\)-degree polynomial whose roots correspond exactly to the matrix eigenvalues.
  • Optimization Test: A continuous function \(f(x)\) possesses a local maximum at a stationary point \(x_c\) if \(f'(x_c) = 0\) and \(f''(x_c) < 0\).

We have a set of \(3\) linear equations in \(3\) unknowns. `\(X \equiv Y\)' means \(X\) and \(Y\) are equivalent statements and `\(X \not\equiv Y\)' means \(X\) and \(Y\) are not equivalent statements.
  • P: There is a unique solution.
  • Q: The equations are linearly independent.
  • R: All eigenvalues of the coefficient matrix are nonzero.
  • S: The determinant of the coefficient matrix is nonzero.
Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.explanation: If there is a unique solution, then \(|A| \neq 0\). All the eigenvalues of \(A\) are non-zero and the given equations are linearly independent. \[\therefore P \equiv Q \equiv R \equiv S\] \[\boxed{\text{(A) $P \equiv Q \equiv R \equiv S$}}\]

questions.question: The volume enclosed by the surface \(f(x,y)=e^x\) over the triangle bounded by the lines \(x=y\), \(x=0\) and \(y=1\) in the \(xy\) plane is .
questions.explanation: The required volume is \[V=\iint_R e^x\,dA\] The region is bounded by \[x=y,\qquad x=0,\qquad y=1\] Hence, the limits are \[0\le y\le 1,\qquad 0\le x\le y\] Therefore, \[V=\int_0^1 \int_0^y e^x\,dx\,dy\] Integrating with respect to \(x\), \[V=\int_0^1 \left[e^x\right]_0^y dy\] \[=\int_0^1 (e^y-1)\,dy\] \[=\left[e^y-y\right]_0^1\] \[=(e-1)-1\] \[=e-2=0.71\] \[\boxed{0.71}\]

questions.question: A solution of the ordinary differential equation \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dt^2}+ 5\dfrac{dy}{dt}+6y=0\) is such that \(y(0)=2\) and \(y(1)=-\dfrac{1-3e}{e^3}.\) The value of \(\dfrac{dy}{dt}(0)\) is .
questions.explanation:
The given differential equation is \[\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} + 5\frac{dy}{dt} + 6y = 0\ \ \text{with the conditions}\ \ y(0) = 2,\ y(1) = -\frac{1-3e}{e^3}.\] We are required to determine \(\left.\dfrac{dy}{dt}\right|_{t=0}.\) Assume a solution of the form \(y = e^{mt}.\) Substituting into the differential equation, we obtain auxiliary equation as \[m^2 + 5m + 6 = 0\] \[(m+2)(m+3) = 0\] Hence, the characteristic roots are \(m_1 = -2,\ m_2 = -3.\) Since the roots are real and distinct, the general solution is \[y = C_1e^{-2t}+C_2e^{-3t}\] Using \(y(0)=2\), \[C_1 + C_2 = 2\] Using \(y(1) = -\dfrac{1-3e}{e^3} = -e^{-3}+3e^{-2},\) \[C_1e^{-2} + C_2e^{-3} = -e^{-3}+3e^{-2}.\] On comparing, \(C_1 = 3,\ C_2 = -1.\) Therefore, \[y = 3e^{-2t}-e^{-3t}.\] Differentiating, \[\frac{dy}{dt} = -6e^{-2t} + 3e^{-3t}\] Hence, \[\left.\frac{dy}{dt}\right|_{t=0} = -6 +3 = -3.\] Therefore, \[\boxed{-3}\]
Key points
  • Distinct roots \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) give the solution \(y = C_1e^{m_1t} + C_2e^{m_2t}.\)

questions.question: A differential equation \(\dfrac{di}{dt}-0.2i=0\) is applicable over \(-10<t<10.\) If \(i(4)=10,\) then \(i(-5)\) is .
questions.explanation:
The differential equation is \[\frac{di}{dt} - 0.2\,i = 0,\ \ -10 < t < 10,\ \ \text{with the condition}\ \ i(4) = 10\] We are required to find the value of \(i(-5).\)
Method 1
The equation is separable: \[\frac{di}{dt} = 0.2\,i\] \[\frac{di}{i} = 0.2\,dt\] Integrating both sides, \[\int \frac{di}{i} = \int 0.2\,dt,\] \[\ln|i| = 0.2t + C\] \[\Rightarrow\ i = e^{0.2t} \times e^C,\] Using the condition \(i(4) = 10\), \[10 = e^{0.8} \times e^C\] \[e^C = 10\,e^{-0.8}\] Therefore, \[i(t) = e^{0.2t} \times 10\,e^{-0.8} = 10\,e^{0.2(t-4)}.\] At \(t=-5\), \[i(-5) = 10\,e^{0.2(-5-4)} = 10\,e^{-1.8}\] \[i(-5)\approx 1.652.\]
Method 2
Using the exponential growth property, \[i(t) = i(t_0)\,e^{0.2(t-t_0)}\] Taking \(t_0 = 4,\ i(t_0) = 10\) \[i(t) = 10\,e^{0.2(t-4)}.\] Therefore, \[i(-5) = 10\,e^{0.2(-9)} = 10\,e^{-1.8} \approx 1.652.\] This method directly uses the known value at \(t=4\) and avoids finding the integration constant explicitly.
Thus, \[\boxed{1.652}\]
Key points
  • This exponential growth form is frequently used in RC/RL circuits, population models, and first-order dynamic systems.

questions.question: Given \(f(z) = g(z) + h(z)\), where \(f, g, h\) are complex valued functions of a complex variable \(z\). Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: If \(f(z)\) is differentiable at \(z_0\), then \(g(z)\) and \(h(z)\) are also differentiable at \(z_0\).
If \(g(z)\) and \(h(z)\) are differentiable at \(z_0\), then \(f(z)\) is also differentiable at \(z_0\).
If \(f(z)\) is continuous at \(z_0\), then it is differentiable at \(z_0\).
If \(f(z)\) is differentiable at \(z_0\), then so are its real and imaginary parts.
questions.explanation:
Given a complex function \(f(z)\) defined as the sum of two other complex functions, \(g(z)\) and \(h(z)\), such that \[f(z)=g(z)+h(z).\] Differentiability Rules for Sums of Complex Functions
In complex analysis, a fundamental property states that if two complex functions, say \(g(z)\) and \(h(z)\), are both differentiable at a point \(z_{0}\), then their sum, \[f(z)=g(z)+h(z),\] is also differentiable at \(z_{0}\). Furthermore, the derivative of the sum is the sum of the derivatives: \[f'(z_{0})=g'(z_{0})+h'(z_{0}).\] If \(g'(z_{0})\) and \(h'(z_{0})\) exist, then \(f'(z_{0})\) exists and \[f'(z_{0})=g'(z_{0})+h'(z_{0}).\] Option A: If \(f(z)\) is differentiable at \(z_{0}\), then \(g(z)\) and \(h(z)\) are also differentiable at \(z_{0}\). False. While \(f(z)\) being differentiable implies certain conditions on its components, it does not guarantee that each individual component function must be differentiable. For example, consider \[f(z)=z.\] This function is differentiable everywhere. We can write \[f(z)=\operatorname{Re}(z)+i\cdot \operatorname{Im}(z).\] Let \[g(z)=\operatorname{Re}(z)=x\] and \[h(z)=i\cdot \operatorname{Im}(z)=iy.\] Here, \[f(z)=g(z)+h(z).\] While \(f(z)\) and \(h(z)\) are differentiable, \(g(z)=x\) is not complex differentiable (its partial derivative with respect to \(y\) is zero, violating the Cauchy--Riemann equations). Therefore, knowing \(f(z)\) is differentiable doesn't force both \(g(z)\) and \(h(z)\) to be differentiable. Option B: If \(g(z)\) and \(h(z)\) are differentiable at \(z_{0}\), then \(f(z)\) is also differentiable at \(z_{0}\). True. Following sum rule for differentiation in complex analysis: If the derivatives \(g'(z_{0})\) and \(h'(z_{0})\) exist, then the derivative of their sum, \(f'(z_{0})\), also exists and is equal to \[g'(z_{0})+h'(z_{0}).\] Option C: If \(f(z)\) is continuous at \(z_{0}\), then it is differentiable at \(z_{0}\). False.A function must be continuous at a point to be differentiable there, but the reverse is not true. Example,\[f(z)=|z|,\] which is continuous everywhere but not differentiable at \[z=0.\] Option D: If \(f(z)\) is differentiable at \(z_{0}\), then so are its real and imaginary parts. If \[f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y),\] differentiability of \(f(z)\) implies that the real-valued functions \(u(x,y)\) and \(v(x,y)\) are real differentiable (i.e., their partial derivatives exist and satisfy the Cauchy--Riemann equations). However, the statement might imply that the complex-valued functions \(u(x,y)\) and \(v(x,y)\) are themselves complex differentiable. This is not necessarily true. For \[f(z)=z=x+iy,\] we have \[u(x,y)=x, \qquad v(x,y)=y.\] Neither \(u\) nor \(v\) is complex differentiable on its own. \[\boxed{\text{B. If $g(z)$ and $h(z)$ are differentiable at $z_0$, then $f(z)$ is also differentiable at $z_0$.} }\]

questions.question: Two coins \(R\) and \(S\) are tossed. The \(4\) joint events \(H_RH_S\), \(T_RT_S\), \(H_RT_S\), \(T_RH_S\) have probabilities \(0.28\), \(0.18\), \(0.30\), \(0.24\) respectively, where \(H\) represents head and \(T\) represents tail. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.explanation: Given joint probabilities: \[P(H_RH_S)=0.28\] \[P(T_RT_S)=0.18\] \[P(H_RT_S)=0.30\] \[P(T_RH_S)=0.24\] First find marginal probabilities for coin \(R\): \[P(H_R)=P(H_RH_S)+P(H_RT_S)\] \[=0.28+0.30=0.58\] \[P(T_R)=0.24+0.18=0.42\] Hence, coin \(R\) is not fair. Now for coin \(S\): \[P(H_S)=P(H_RH_S)+P(T_RH_S)\] \[=0.28+0.24=0.52\] \[P(T_S)=0.30+0.18=0.48\] Hence, coin \(S\) is also not fair. To check independence: \[P(H_RH_S)\stackrel{?}{=}P(H_R)P(H_S)\] \[0.28 \stackrel{?}{=} (0.58)(0.52)\] \[0.28 \neq 0.3016\] Therefore, the tosses are dependent. \[\boxed{\text{(d) The coin tosses are dependent}}\]

Let \(P\) be the probability that player \(A\) wins the game. Player \(A\) wins immediately if he gets a six in the first throw. \[P(\text{$A$ wins in first turn})=\frac16\] If both \(A\) and \(B\) fail to get a six in their respective turns, the game returns to the original situation. \[P(\text{both fail})
=
\frac56 \times \frac56
=
\frac{25}{36}\] Hence, \[P=\frac16+\frac{25}{36}P\] Solving, \[P\left(1-\frac{25}{36}\right)=\frac16\] \[P\cdot \frac{11}{36}=\frac16\] \[P=\frac16 \times \frac{36}{11}\] \[P=\frac{6}{11}\] \[\boxed{\text{(d) }\dfrac{6}{11}}\]

questions.question: If a continuous function \(f(x)\) does not have a root in the interval \([a, b]\), then which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Let \(f(x)\) be a continuous function bounded on the closed interval \([a, b]\).
  • According to the Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT) and Rolle's base premises, if a continuous function transitions across a real root inside \([a, b]\), the function values at the boundaries must have opposite signs (\(f(a) \cdot f(b) < 0\)).
  • Conversely, if the function **does not have a root** anywhere in the interval \([a, b]\), it cannot cross the \(x\)-axis. Therefore, the function must remain entirely on one side of the axis across the whole interval.
  • Since \(f(x)\) preserves its sign throughout the interval, \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) must share identical polarities (either both positive or both negative).
  • Multiplying two values with matching mathematical signs always outputs a strictly positive product: \(f(a) \cdot f(b) > 0\).
\[\boxed{\text{C. } f(a) \cdot f(b) > 0}\]
Key points
  • Intermediate Value Theorem Contrapositive: If a continuous function satisfies \(f(a) \cdot f(b) \le 0\), it is guaranteed to possess at least one real root inside the interval \([a, b]\). Therefore, the total absence of a root guarantees that \(f(a) \cdot f(b) > 0\).

questions.question: The circuit shown in the figure has two sources connected in series. The instantaneous voltage of the AC source (in Volt) is given by v(t) = 12 sin t. If the circuit is in steady state, then the RMS value of the current (in Ampere) flowing in the circuit is .
questions.explanation:
The total root-mean-square (RMS) response of a multi-frequency network containing independent linear AC and DC excitations can be calculated using the principle of superposition. Case 1: Under the action of the \(8\,\text{V}\) DC source acting alone
For a pure DC excitation, the steady-state operating frequency is \(\omega_1 = 0\,\text{rad/s}\). At this zero frequency condition, the reactive response of any network inductance transitions to zero: \[X_{L1} = \omega_1 L = 0 \times 1 = 0\,\Omega\] Hence, the inductor acts as an ideal short circuit. Assuming a basic loop path configuration with a series resistance of \(1\,\Omega\), the resulting DC current component is given by: \[I_{dc} = \frac{8}{1} = 8\,\text{A}\] Case 2: Under the action of the \(12\sin(t)\,\text{V}\) sinusoidal source acting alone
The operating frequency for this independent excitation is \(\omega_2 = 1\,\text{rad/s}\). The inductive reactance at this specific frequency is calculated as: \[X_{L2} = \omega_2 L = 1 \times 1 = 1\,\Omega\] The complex impedance of the series \(RL\) branch layout is: \[Z = R + jX_{L2} = 1 + j1\,\Omega\] Expressing the total impedance in polar form yields: \[Z = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2}\angle\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1}\right) = \sqrt{2}\angle 45^\circ\,\Omega\] The corresponding AC phasor current component is evaluated using Ohm's law: \[I_{ac} = \frac{12\angle 0^\circ}{1 + j1} = \frac{12\angle 0^\circ}{\sqrt{2}\angle 45^\circ} = \frac{12}{\sqrt{2}}\angle -45^\circ\,\text{A}\] Converting the phasor response back into its time-domain equivalent form: \[i_{ac}(t) = \frac{12}{\sqrt{2}}\sin(t - 45^\circ)\,\text{A}\] The RMS value of this specific sinusoidal current component is: \[I_{rms,ac} = \frac{I_{max}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{12/\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{12}{2} = 6\,\text{A}\] Total Effective Current Evaluation:
Since the components originate from independent sources operating at completely distinct frequencies (\(0\,\text{rad/s}\) and \(1\,\text{rad/s}\)), their individual effective root-mean-square values are combined orthogonally: \[I_{rms} = \sqrt{I_{dc}^2 + I_{rms,ac}^2}\] \[I_{rms} = \sqrt{8^2 + \left(\frac{12/ \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} = \sqrt{64 + 6^2} = \sqrt{64 + 36} = \sqrt{100} = 10\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{10}\]
Key points
  • DC Inductor Behavior: Under stable DC excitation conditions (\(\omega = 0\)), the inductive reactance drops to zero (\(X_L = 0\)), reducing the component model down to a basic short circuit path.
  • Multi-Frequency RMS Combination: Total effective current for distinct orthogonal harmonic/DC frequencies cannot be algebraically summed up. The calculation demands a root-sum-square calculation profile: \(I_{rms} = \sqrt{I_0^2 + I_{rms1}^2 + I_{rms2}^2 + \dots}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Remember to divide the maximum peak amplitude of the sinusoidal component (\(I_{max} = 12/\sqrt{2}\,\text{A}\)) by \(\sqrt{2}\) to convert it accurately into its standalone \(I_{rms}\) value before squaring it inside the final radical expression.

questions.question: An inductor is connected in parallel with a capacitor as shown in the figure. As the frequency of current i is increased, the impedance (Z) of the network varies as
questions.explanation:
The total equivalent input impedance \(Z\) of two parallel branches is calculated using the standard parallel product-over-sum formula: \[Z = \frac{(j\omega L) \cdot \left(\frac{1}{j\omega C}\right)}{j\omega L + \frac{1}{j\omega C}}\] Simplifying the numerator: \[(j\omega L) \cdot \left(\frac{1}{j\omega C}\right) = \frac{L}{C}\] Simplifying the denominator by finding a common base: \[j\omega L + \frac{1}{j\omega C} = \frac{(j\omega L)(j\omega C) + 1}{j\omega C} = \frac{-\omega^{2}LC + 1}{j\omega C} = \frac{j(1 - \omega^{2}LC)}{-\omega C} = j\left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)\] Substituting these components back into the main expression for \(Z\): \[Z = \frac{\frac{L}{C}}{j\left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)} = \frac{L}{jC\left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)} = \frac{-jL}{\omega LC - \frac{C}{\omega C}} = \frac{-j\omega L}{\omega^{2}LC - 1}\] Multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by \(-1\) gives: \[Z = \frac{j\omega L}{1 - \omega^{2}LC}\] Dividing both the numerator and denominator by \(LC\): \[Z = \frac{\frac{j\omega L}{LC}}{\frac{1}{LC} - \omega^{2}} = \frac{j\left(\frac{\omega}{C}\right)}{\frac{1}{LC} - \omega^{2}}\] We analyze the behavior of the input network based on the operating angular frequency \(\omega\) relative to the anti-resonant frequency \(\omega_{o} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\):
  • Case 1: Sub-resonant Region \(\left(\omega < \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\right)\)
    When the frequency is low, \(\omega^{2} < \frac{1}{LC}\), which makes the denominator of Z positive: \[Z = \frac{j\left(\frac{\omega}{C}\right)}{\frac{1}{LC} - \omega^{2}}\] Thus, the parallel network displays a purely inductive property.
  • Case 2: Super-resonant Region \(\left(\omega > \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\right)\)
    When the frequency is high, \(\omega^{2} > \frac{1}{LC}\), which makes the denominator of Z negative: \[Z = \frac{-j\left(\frac{\omega}{C}\right)}{\omega^{2} - \frac{1}{LC}}\] Thus, the parallel network displays a purely capacitive property.
  • Case 3: Ideal Anti-resonance condition \(\left(\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\right)\)
    At this precise threshold frequency, the denominator value equals zero: \[\omega^{2} - \frac{1}{LC} = 0 \implies Z \to \infty\]
\[\boxed{(b)}\]

questions.question: In a linear two-port network, when \(10\,\text{V}\) is applied to port 1, a current of \(4\,\text{A}\) flows through port 2 when it is short -- circuited. When \(5\,\text{V}\) is applied to port 1, a current of \(1.25\,\text{A}\) flows through a \(1\,\Omega\) resistance connected across port 2. When \(3\,\text{V}\) is applied to port 1, the current (in Ampere) through a \(2\,\Omega\) resistance connected across port 2 is .
questions.explanation: The standard transmission parameters relate the input variables to the output variables via the following equation: \[V_1 = A V_2 + B I_2\] (Note: Here, \(I_2\) is defined as flowing out of the port.) 1. Condition 1: Port-2 is Short-Circuited (\(V_2 = 0\)) Given that \(V_1 = 10\,\text{V}\) and the measured output short-circuit current is \(I_2 = 4\,\text{A}\): \[V_1 = B I_2 \implies 10 = B \times 4\] \[B = 2.5\,\Omega\] 2. Condition 2: A Resistance of \(1\,\Omega\) is Connected at Port-2 When a \(1\,\Omega\) load resistor is attached, the output voltage is given by Ohm's law: \[V_2 = 1 \times I_2 = I_2\] Given that the input voltage is \(V_1 = 5\,\text{V}\) and the current is \(I_2 = 1.25\,\text{A}\): \[5 = (A + B) I_2 \implies 5 = (A + B) \times 1.25\] \[A + B = \frac{5}{1.25} = 4\] Substituting the value of \(B = 2.5\,\Omega\): \[A + 2.5 = 4 \implies A = 1.5\] 3. Condition 3: A Resistance of \(2\,\Omega\) is Connected at Port-2 When a \(2\,\Omega\) load resistor is connected, the relationship becomes: \[V_2 = 2 I_2\] Given that the input voltage is \(V_1 = 3\,\text{V}\), we substitute \(V_2\) into the primary transmission parameter equation: \[V_1 = A (2 I_2) + B I_2 \implies V_1 = (2 A + B) I_2\] Solving for the terminal output current \(I_2\): \[I_2 = \frac{V_1}{2 A + B}\] Substituting the evaluated parameters \(A = 1.5\) and \(B = 2.5\,\Omega\), along with \(V_1 = 3\,\text{V}\): \[I_2 = \frac{3}{(2 \times 1.5) + 2.5} = \frac{3}{3 + 2.5} = \frac{3}{5.5} \approx 0.5454\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{0.5454}\]

questions.question: For linear time invariant systems, that are Bounded Input Bounded Output stable, which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The impulse response will be integrable, but may not be absolutely integrable.
The unit impulse response will have finite support.
The unit step response will be absolutely integrable.
The unit step response will be bounded.
questions.explanation:
For a continuous-time LTI system, the necessary and sufficient condition for BIBO stability is \[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(t)|\,dt<\infty,\] i.e., the impulse response must be absolutely integrable. Since the input \(u(t)\) is bounded (\(|u(t)|\le 1\)), the corresponding output is the step response \[s(t)=h(t)*u(t).\] For a BIBO stable system, \[|s(t)| =\left|\int_{-\infty}^{t}h(\tau)\,d\tau\right| \le \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(\tau)|\,d\tau <\infty.\] Hence, the unit step response is always bounded. Checking the options:
  • A. False: BIBO stability requires absolute integrability of \(h(t)\).
  • B. False: The impulse response need not have finite support.
  • C. False: The step response is not necessarily absolutely integrable.
  • D. True: The unit step response is bounded.
\[\boxed{\text{(d) The unit step response will be bounded.}}\]

questions.question:
The signum function is given by \[\operatorname{sgn}(x)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{x}{|x|}, & x\neq 0,\\
0, & x=0.
\end{cases}\] The Fourier series expansion of \(\operatorname{sgn}(\cos(t))\) has
options: only sine terms with all harmonics.
only cosine terms with all harmonics.
only sine terms with even numbered harmonics.
only cosine terms with odd numbered harmonics.
questions.explanation:
Given, \[\operatorname{sgn}(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{x}{|x|}, & x\neq0,\\ 0, & x=0. \end{cases}\] The signal is \[f(t)=\operatorname{sgn}(\cos t).\] Since \[\cos(-t)=\cos t,\] we have \[f(-t)=\operatorname{sgn}(\cos(-t)) =\operatorname{sgn}(\cos t)=f(t).\] Hence, \(f(t)\) is an even function, so its Fourier series contains only cosine terms. Also, \[f(t+\pi)=\operatorname{sgn}(\cos(t+\pi)) =-\operatorname{sgn}(\cos t) =-f(t).\] Thus, the signal has half-wave symmetry, which eliminates all even harmonics. Therefore, the Fourier series contains only odd cosine harmonics: \[f(t)=\frac{4}{\pi}\left( \cos t-\frac{1}{3}\cos3t+\frac{1}{5}\cos5t-\cdots \right).\] \[\boxed{\text{(d) Only cosine terms with odd numbered harmonics}}\]
Key points
  • Even symmetry \(\Rightarrow\) only cosine coefficients are present.
  • Half-wave symmetry \(\bigl(f(t+\pi)=-f(t)\bigr)\) eliminates all even harmonics.
  • The Fourier series of \(\operatorname{sgn}(\cos t)\) contains only odd cosine harmonics.

questions.explanation:
Filter \(F_1\) is a low-pass filter with cut-off frequency \(f_1\), while \(F_2\) is a high-pass filter with cut-off frequency \(f_2\). The op-amp is a differential amplifier with equal input resistors \(R\) and feedback resistor \(R/2\). Hence, \[v_o=\frac{R/2}{R}\left(v_{F2}-v_{F1}\right) =\frac{1}{2}\left(v_{F2}-v_{F1}\right).\] Now consider different frequency ranges:
  • For \(f<f_1\): \(F_1\) passes and \(F_2\) blocks, so \(v_o\neq0\).
  • For \(f_1<f<f_2\): both filters attenuate the signal, so \(v_o\approx0\).
  • For \(f>f_2\): \(F_2\) passes and \(F_1\) blocks, so \(v_o\neq0\).
Thus, the circuit attenuates only the middle band and passes both low and high frequencies. Therefore, it behaves as a band-stop (notch) filter. \[\boxed{\text{(b) Band-stop filter}}\]

questions.question:
Of the four characteristics given below, which are the major requirements for an instrumentation amplifier?
  • P. High common mode rejection ratio
  • Q. High input impedance
  • R. High linearity
  • S. High output impedance
questions.explanation:
• An ideal Instrumentation Amplifier features extremely high CMRR, high input impedance, high linearity, and low output impedance to prevent loading effects.
  • Why Low Output Impedance (\(Z_{\text{out}} \approx 0\))?
    • Minimizes Loading Effect: Prevents voltage attenuation across internal resistance when connected to a load (\(R_L\)): \[V_L = V_{\text{internal}} \times \frac{R_L}{R_{\text{out}} + R_L} \approx V_{\text{internal}} \quad (\text{for } R_{\text{out}} \ll R_L)\]
    • Ensures Gain Stability: Maintains linear output voltage regardless of load variations.
    • Current Drive Capability: Supplies required load current to downstream stages (ADCs, filters) without signal droop.
\[\boxed{\text{(A) P, Q and R only}}\]

questions.question: Consider the circuit shown in the figure. In this circuit \(R = 1\text{ k}\Omega\), and \(C = 1\ \mu\text{F}\). The input voltage is sinusoidal with a frequency of \(50\text{ Hz}\), represented as a phasor with magnitude \(V_i\) and phase angle \(0\) radian as shown in the figure. The output voltage is represented as a phasor with magnitude \(V_o\) and phase angle \(\delta\) radian. What is the value of the output phase angle \(\delta\) (in radian) relative to the phase angle of the input voltage?
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Using Superposition Principle:
Output due to inverting input: \[V_{o1} = V_1 \left[\frac{-R}{1 / (Cs)}\right] = -s C R V_1\] Potential at non-inverting node: \[V_+ = V_2 \left[\frac{R}{R + 1 / (Cs)}\right]\] Output due to non-inverting input: \[V_{o2} = (1 + R C s) \times \frac{R}{R + 1 / (Cs)} \times V_1 = s C R V_2\] Total output voltage: \[V_o = V_{o1} + V_{o2} = -s C R (V_1 - V_2) = -s C R V_i\] Substitute \(s = j\omega = j(100\pi)\): \[V_o = -j(100\pi)(10^{-6})(10^3)V_i = -j(0.1\pi)V_i\] \[V_o = 0.1\pi V_i \angle -90^\circ \implies \delta = -90^\circ = -\frac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}\]
Method 2
Using KVL and Virtual Short Concept: img/ch3_operational_amplifier/3_15_2.png By virtual short, \(V_A = V_B\). KVL in the input loop from node \(A\) to \(B\): \[I\left(\frac{1}{sC}\right) - V_i + I\left(\frac{1}{sC}\right) = 0 \implies I = \frac{V_i(sC)}{2}\] \[V_A = -I R = -\frac{s C R V_i}{2} = V_B\] Current relation at output node: \[\frac{V_B - V_o}{R} = I \implies V_o = V_B - I R\] \[V_o = -\frac{V_i(sC R)}{2} - \frac{V_i(sC R)}{2} = -s C R V_i\] For \(s = j\omega\): \(V_o = -j\omega R C V_i\), which lags \(V_i\) by \(90^\circ\). \[\delta = -\frac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}\]
\[\boxed{(D) \ \ -{\pi}/{2}}\]
Key points
Phasor Angle: Multiplication by \(-j = 1\angle -90^\circ\) corresponds to a phase delay of \(90^\circ\) (\(-\frac{\pi}{2}\text{ rad}\)).

questions.question: The operational amplifier shown in the figure is ideal. The input voltage (in Volt) is \(V_i = 2 \sin(2\pi \times 2000t)\). The amplitude of the output voltage \(V_o\) (in Volt) is
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Given \(V_i = 2 \sin(2\pi \times 2000t) \implies \omega = 4000\pi\text{ rad/s}\). Capacitive reactance: \[X_c = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{4000\pi \times 0.1 \times 10^{-6}} = 795.77\,\Omega\] Equivalent feedback impedance (\(Z_{\text{eq}}\)): \[Z_{\text{eq}} = \frac{R \cdot (-j X_c)}{R - j X_c} = 622.67 \angle -51.488^\circ\,\Omega\] Output voltage magnitude: \[V_o = V_{\text{in}} \left( \frac{|Z_{\text{eq}}|}{R_1} \right) = 2 \times \frac{622.67}{1000} = 1.245\,\text{V}\]
Method 2
Transfer function \(H(s)\) of the inverting amplifier: \[H(s) = \frac{-Z_f}{R_1} = \frac{-\left(\frac{R}{R C s + 1}\right)}{R_1} = \frac{-1}{10^{-4} s + 1}\] For \(s = j\omega = j(4000\pi)\): \[|H(j\omega)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (10^{-4} \times 4000\pi)^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (0.4\pi)^2}} \approx 0.6226\] Amplitude of output voltage \(V_o\): \[|V_o| = 2 \times |H(j\omega)| = 2 \times 0.6226 = 1.245\,\text{V}\]
\[\boxed{1.245}\]
Key points
Output Amplitude: The magnitude of output voltage for a sinusoidal input is given by \(|V_o| = V_m \cdot |H(j\omega)|\).

questions.question: The op-amp shown in the figure has a finite gain \(A = 1000\) and an infinite input resistance. A step-voltage \(V_i = 1\text{ mV}\) is applied at the input at time \(t = 0\) as shown. Assuming that the operational amplifier is not saturated, the time constant (in millisecond) of the output voltage \(V_o\) is
questions.explanation:
Since \(V_+ = 0\,\text{V}\), the inverting node voltage \(V_A\) relates to the output as: \[V_o = A(V_+ - V_A) = -1000 V_A \implies V_A = -\frac{V_o}{1000}\] Applying KCL at node \(A\) in the \(s\)-domain: \[\frac{V_A - V_i}{R} + \frac{V_A - V_o}{1 / (s C)} = 0\] \[\frac{V_A - V_i}{1000} = \big(V_A - (-1000 V_A)\big) s C\] \[V_A [1 - 1.001 s] = V_i \implies V_A = \frac{V_i}{1 - 1.001 s}\] Substituting \(V_A = -\dfrac{V_o}{1000}\) gives the overall transfer relation: \[V_o(s) = \frac{-1000}{1 - 1.001 s} V_i(s)\] The time constant \(\tau\) is : \[\tau = 1.001\,\text{s} = 1001\,\text{ms}\] \[\boxed{(A) \ \ 1001}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • For finite Gain Op-Amp: Virtual ground \(V_A \approx 0\) does not hold strictly; instead, \(V_A = -V_o / A\). Avoid assuming ideal virtual ground (\(V_A = 0\)), which incorrectly yields \(\tau = R C = 1\,\text{ms}\).
  • Ensure unit conversion from seconds (\(1.001\,\text{s}\)) to milliseconds (\(1001\,\text{ms}\)).

questions.question: The saturation voltage of the ideal op-amp shown below is \(\pm 10\text{ V}\). The output voltage \(v_0\) of the following circuit in the steady-state is
questions.explanation:
Method 1
The given circuit is an astable multivibrator (square wave generator). Feedback factor \(\beta\): \[\beta = \frac{2\,\text{k}\Omega}{2\,\text{k}\Omega + 2\,\text{k}\Omega} = \frac{2}{4} = 0.5\] Upper and lower threshold voltages: \[V_{\text{UTP}} = +\beta V_{\text{sat}} = +5\,\text{V}, \quad V_{\text{LTP}} = -\beta V_{\text{sat}} = -5\,\text{V}\] Capacitor charging equation for \(V_o = +10\,\text{V}\): \[V_c(t) = V_c(\infty) + [V_c(0) - V_c(\infty)] e^{-t / \tau}\] where \(V_c(\infty) = +10\,\text{V}\), \(V_c(0) = -5\,\text{V}\), and \(\tau = R C = 1\,\text{k}\Omega \times 0.25\,\mu\text{F} = 0.25\,\text{ms}\). \[V_c(t) = 10 - 15 e^{-t / \tau}\] At \(t = T_1\), \(V_c(T_1) = 5\,\text{V}\): \[5 = 10 - 15 e^{-T_1 / \tau} \implies T_1 = \tau \ln 3 = 0.25 \ln 3 \approx 0.275\,\text{ms}\]
Since UTP and LTP are symmetric, the duty cycle is \(50\%\). The total time period \(T\) is: \[T = 2 T_1 = 2 \times 0.275\,\text{ms} = 0.55\,\text{ms}\]
Method 2
Direct formula for time period of an astable multivibrator: \[T = 2 R C \ln\left(\frac{1 + \beta}{1 - \beta}\right)\] With \(\beta = 0.5\) and \(R C = 1\,\text{k}\Omega \times 0.25\,\mu\text{F} = 0.25\,\text{ms}\): \[T = 2 \times 0.25 \times \ln\left(\frac{1 + 0.5}{1 - 0.5}\right) = 0.5 \ln(3) \approx 0.55\,\text{ms}\] Since the output is taken at node \(V_o\) of the op-amp, it switches between \(+V_{\text{sat}}\) and \(-V_{\text{sat}}\), producing a square wave.
\[\boxed{\text{(A) square wave of period $0.55\text{ ms}$.}}\]

questions.explanation: Analyzing gain at extreme frequency limits: At \(\omega \to 0\) (Low Frequencies): \[H_1(0) = 1, \quad H_2(0) = 0 \implies \left|\frac{V_o}{V_i}\right| \neq 0 \text{ (Passes)}\] At \(\omega \to \infty\) (High Frequencies): \[H_1(\infty) = 0, \quad H_2(\infty) = 1 \implies \left|\frac{V_o}{V_i}\right| \neq 0 \text{ (Passes)}\] At mid-band frequencies (\(f_1 < f < f_2\)): \[H_1(f) \approx 0, \quad H_2(f) \approx 0 \implies \left|\frac{V_o}{V_i}\right| \approx 0 \text{ (Stops)}\] Since low and high frequencies pass while mid-band frequencies are rejected, the overall response represents a Band-stop filter. \[\boxed{\text{(B) Band-stop filter}}\]

questions.question: In the given circuit, the silicon transistor has \(\beta = 75\) and a collector voltage \(V_C = 9\,\text{V}\). Then the ratio of \(R_B\) and \(R_C\) is .
questions.explanation:
Given: \(\beta = 75\), \(V_C = 9\,\text{V}\) Here we take \(V_{BE} = 0.7\,\text{V}\). Applying KVL in loop (1), \[-15 + I_B(\beta + 1)R_C + 9 = 0\] \[I_B(\beta + 1)R_C = 6\,\text{V} \quad \dots \text{(i)}\] Applying KVL in loop (2), \[-15 + I_B(\beta + 1)R_C + I_B R_B + 0.7 = 0\] From equation (i), \[-15 + 6 + I_B R_B + 0.7 = 0\] \[I_B R_B = 8.3\,\text{V} \quad \dots \text{(ii)}\] From equation (i) and (ii), \[\frac{I_B R_B}{I_B(\beta + 1)R_C} = \frac{8.3}{6}\] \[\frac{R_B}{R_C} = \frac{8.3}{6} \times (75 + 1) = 105.13\] \[\boxed{105.13}\]
Key points
  • In a collector-to-base feedback bias circuit, the total current through \(R_C\) is \(I_C + I_B = (\beta + 1)I_B\).
  • Expressing the loop equations allows solving for the ratio \(\frac{R_B}{R_C}\) directly without determining \(I_B\) individually.

Given fixed bias circuit is shown below, Given transistor is in active region because \(V_{CE} > 0.2\,\text{V}\) when \(V_C = 2\,\text{V}\) and \(V_C = 4\,\text{V}\). Applying KVL in loop (1), \[-10 + R_B I_B + V_{BE} = 0\] \[I_B = \frac{10 - V_{BE}}{R_B}\] Collector current is given by, \[I_C = \beta I_B\] Since, change in \(R_C\) does not affect the base current \(I_B\) as well as \(I_C\). Thus, collector current \(I_C = \text{constant}\). Applying KVL in loop (2), \[-10 + I_C R_C + V_C = 0\] \[I_C = \frac{10 - V_C}{R_C} \quad \dots \text{(i)}\] For \(V_C = 2\,\text{V}\) ,
From equation (i), \[I_C = \frac{10 - 2}{R_C} = \frac{8}{R_C} \quad \dots \text{(ii)}\] For \(V_C = 4\,\text{V}\) ,
\[I_C = \frac{10 - V_C}{R_C'} = \frac{10 - 4}{R_C'} = \frac{6}{R_C'} \quad \dots \text{(iii)}\] From equation (ii) and (iii), \[\frac{R_C'}{R_C} = \frac{6}{8} = 0.75\] \[\boxed{0.75}\]
Key points

  • Equating expressions for \(I_C\) under two different collector voltages yields the required resistance ratio directly.

questions.question: The figure shows a digital circuit constructed using negative edge triggered \(J\)-\(K\) flip flops. Assume a starting state of \(Q_2\,Q_1\,Q_0 = 000\) will repeat after number of cycles of the clock.
questions.explanation:
Given: Logic circuit is shown below, As per the question, all the \(J-K\) flip-flops are negative-edge triggered. To analyze this asynchronous circuit properly, we must track the specific triggering conditions for each stage:
  • FF0 Clock: Driven directly by the main clock (\(\text{CLK}\)). Since \(J_0 = K_0 = 1\), \(Q_0\) toggles on every single falling edge (\(\downarrow\)) of \(\text{CLK}\).
  • FF1 & FF2 Clocks: Both clock pins are tied directly to the output \(Q_0\). Therefore, FF1 and FF2 can update only when \(Q_0\) undergoes a falling edge transition (\(1 \to 0\)). On a rising edge of \(Q_0\) (\(0 \to 1\)), they are not triggered and strictly hold their previous states regardless of input values.
Evaluating the circuit edge-by-edge starting from the initial state \(Q_2 Q_1 Q_0 = 000\), we construct the true asynchronous state table, explicitly tracing the synchronous steering lines \(J_1 = \bar{Q}_2\), \(K_1 = 1\), \(J_2 = Q_1\), and \(K_2 = 1\):
Clock PulseTransition of \(Q_0\)\(J_1\)\(K_1\)\(J_2\)\(K_2\)FF1 ActionFF2 ActionNext State (\(Q_2 Q_1 Q_0\))
Initially———————\(000\)
\(1^{\text{st}}\) (\(\downarrow\) \(\text{CLK}\))\(0 \to 1\) (Rising Edge)1101Hold StateHold State\(001\)
\(2^{\text{nd}}\) (\(\downarrow\) \(\text{CLK}\))\(1 \to 0\) (Falling Edge)1101ToggleReset\(010\)
\(3^{\text{rd}}\) (\(\downarrow\) \(\text{CLK}\))\(0 \to 1\) (Rising Edge)1111Hold StateHold State\(011\)
\(4^{\text{th}}\) (\(\downarrow\) \(\text{CLK}\))\(1 \to 0\) (Falling Edge)1111ToggleToggle\(100\)
\(5^{\text{th}}\) (\(\downarrow\) \(\text{CLK}\))\(0 \to 1\) (Rising Edge)0101Hold StateHold State\(101\)
\(6^{\text{th}}\) (\(\downarrow\) \(\text{CLK}\))\(1 \to 0\) (Falling Edge)0101ResetReset\(000\)
From the state table, we can map out the corresponding state diagram: Thus, the state vector \(Q_2 Q_1 Q_0\) returns to its initial configuration after exactly 6 complete clock cycles of the main clock, confirming that it functions as a mod-6 counter sequence. Detailed Behavioral Analysis:
  1. First active trigger of secondary stages (CLK 2): When \(Q_0\) drops from \(1 \to 0\), both FF1 and FF2 are clocked. Evaluating inputs based on the previous state (\(001\)):
    • For FF1: \(J_1 = \bar{Q}_2 = \bar{0} = 1, K_1 = 1 \implies\) Toggle (\(0 \to 1\)).
    • For FF2: \(J_2 = Q_1 = 0, K_2 = 1 \implies\) Reset (Stays \(0\)).
  2. Second active trigger of secondary stages (CLK 4): When \(Q_0\) drops from \(1 \to 0\) again. Evaluating inputs based on the previous state (\(011\)):
    • For FF1: \(J_1 = \bar{Q}_2 = \bar{0} = 1, K_1 = 1 \implies\) Toggle (\(1 \to 0\)).
    • For FF2: \(J_2 = Q_1 = 1, K_2 = 1 \implies\) Toggle (\(0 \to 1\)).
  3. Third active trigger of secondary stages (CLK 6): When \(Q_0\) drops from \(1 \to 0\) for the final time. Evaluating inputs based on the previous state (\(101\)):
    • For FF1: \(J_1 = \bar{Q}_2 = \bar{1} = 0, K_1 = 1 \implies\) Reset (Stays \(0\)).
    • For FF2: \(J_2 = Q_1 = 0, K_2 = 1 \implies\) Reset (\(1 \to 0\)).
\[\boxed{6}\]
Key points
  • Asynchronous clock cascades require careful evaluation of the specific falling edges (\(\downarrow\)) generated by preceding state transitions.
  • Next-state conditions must always evaluate the current logic level of the control steering lines (\(J, K\)) right before the active clock transition edge hits.
Hence, the answer is \(\mathbf{6}\).

questions.question: An 8-bit unipolar successive approximation register type ADC is used to convert 3.5,V to digital equivalent output. The reference voltage is \(+5\),V. The output of ADC at the end of 3rd clock pulse after the start of conversion is
questions.explanation:
Given:
  • Number of bits: \(n = 8\)
  • Input voltage: \(V_a = 3.5\,\text{V}\)
  • Reference voltage: \(V_{ref} = +5\,\text{V}\)
Method 1
Step-by-step SAR algorithm:
Resolution: \[R = \frac{V_{FS}}{2^n - 1} = \frac{5}{2^8 - 1} = \frac{5}{255} \approx 0.0196\,\text{V}\] 1st clock pulse: MSB is set. \[\text{Output} = (10000000)_2 = (128)_{10}\] \[V_C = 128 \times \frac{5}{255} = 2.5098\,\text{V}\] Since \(V_0 < V_a\) (i.e., \(2.5098 < 3.5\)), MSB remains set (1). 2nd clock pulse: Next MSB is set. \[\text{Output} = (11000000)_2 = (192)_{10}\] \[V_C = 192 \times \frac{5}{255} = 3.7647\,\text{V}\] Since \(V_0 > V_a\) (i.e., \(3.7647 > 3.5\)), 2nd MSB is reset (0). 3rd clock pulse: Next bit is set. \[\text{Output} = (10100000)_2 = (160)_{10}\] \[V_C = 160 \times \frac{5}{255} = 3.137\,\text{V}\] Since \(V_0 < V_a\) (i.e., \(3.137 < 3.5\)), 3rd MSB remains set (1). Therefore, the output after the 3rd clock pulse is: \[\boxed{10100000}\]
Method 2
Using the SAR algorithm flowchart:
This method interprets the same SAR conversion process using the binary-search concept. The comparison voltages (\(2.5098\,\text{V}\), \(3.7647\,\text{V}\), \(3.137\,\text{V}\)) are the DAC outputs corresponding to the trial codes generated by the SAR register in Method 1. The SAR ADC uses a binary search algorithm. Starting from \(V_{ref}/2\) each time:
  • Clock 1: Compare \(3.5\,\text{V}\) vs \(2.51\,\text{V}\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(V_a > V_C\) \(\Rightarrow\) bit 7 = 1 \(\Rightarrow\) 10000000
  • Clock 2: Compare \(3.5\,\text{V}\) vs \(3.76\,\text{V}\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(V_a < V_C\) \(\Rightarrow\) bit 6 = 0 \(\Rightarrow\) 10000000
  • Clock 3: Compare \(3.5\,\text{V}\) vs \(3.14\,\text{V}\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(V_a > V_C\) \(\Rightarrow\) bit 5 = 1 \(\Rightarrow\) 10100000
(A) 1010 0000
Key points
  • SAR Rule: If \(V_a > V_C\): current bit remains 1, next bit is tested. If \(V_a < V_C\): current bit is reset to 0, next bit is tested.
  • An \(n\)-bit SAR ADC requires exactly \(n\) clock pulses to complete one conversion.
  • Maximum conversion time: \(T_{max} = n \cdot T_{CLK}\)
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use \(2^n\) in the denominator for resolution. The correct formula uses \(2^n - 1\) for unipolar ADCs.
  • The algorithm continues even after resetting a bit --- the next lower bit is always tested in the subsequent clock cycle.

questions.question: An open loop control system results in a response of \(e^{-2t}(\sin 5t + \cos 5t)\) for a unit impulse input. The DC gain of the control system is
questions.explanation: Given the impulse response of an open-loop control system: \(g(t) = e^{-2t}(\sin 5t + \cos 5t)\) The transfer function \(G(s)\) is the Laplace transform of the impulse response: \[G(s) = \frac{5}{(s+2)^2 + 5^2} + \frac{s+2}{(s+2)^2 + 5^2}\] The DC gain of the control system is defined as the value of the transfer function at \(s = 0\): \[\text{DC gain} = \left. G(s) \right|_{s = 0}\] Substituting \(s = 0\) into the equation: \[G(0) = \frac{5}{2^2 + 5^2} + \frac{2}{2^2 + 5^2} = \frac{5}{29} + \frac{2}{29} = \frac{7}{29} \approx 0.241\] \[\boxed{0.241}\]

questions.question: The unit step response of a system with the transfer function \(G(s) = \dfrac{1-2s}{1+s}\) is given by which one of the following waveforms?
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Let the unit step response be \(y(t)\). \[G(s) = \frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}\] \[Y(s) = \left(\frac{1}{s}\right)\left(\frac{1-2s}{1+s}\right)\] \[Y(s) = \frac{1+s-3s}{s(1+s)} = \frac{1}{s} - \frac{3}{1+s}\] Taking the inverse Laplace transform: \[y(t) = \mathcal{L}^{-1}[Y(s)]\] \[y(t) = (1 - 3e^{-t})u(t)\] The waveform of \(y(t)\) starts at \(-2\) when \(t=0\), and reaches \(1\) as \(t \to \infty\).
Method 2
The Laplace transform of the output response is: \[Y(s) = \frac{1-2s}{s(1+s)}\] Applying the Initial Value Theorem to find \(y(0^+)\): \[\lim_{t \to 0^+} y(t) = \lim_{s \to \infty} sY(s)\] \[\lim_{t \to 0^+} y(t) = \lim_{s \to \infty} \left[ \frac{1-2s}{1+s} \right] = -2\] Only the waveform in option (A) satisfies this initial condition.
\[\boxed{(A)}\]

questions.ref: Block Diagram and Signal Flow Graph Q2
questions.question: Find the transfer function \(\dfrac{Y(s)}{X(s)}\) of the system given below.
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Analytical Method
From the block diagram, the system equations are: \[Y(s) = [X(s) - HY(s)]G_1 + [X(s) - HY(s)]G_2\] \[Y(s) = [X(s) - HY(s)][G_1 + G_2]\] \[Y(s)[1 + H(G_1 + G_2)] = X(s)[G_1 + G_2]\] \[\frac{Y(s)}{X(s)} = \frac{G_1 + G_2}{1 + H(G_1 + G_2)}\]
Method 2
Signal Flow Graph (SFG)
  • Forward paths: \(P_1 = G_1, \quad P_2 = G_2\)
  • Individual loops: \(L_1 = -HG_1, \quad L_2 = -HG_2\)
  • Path factors: \(\Delta_1 = 1, \quad \Delta_2 = 1\)
Applying Mason's gain formula: \[\frac{Y(s)}{X(s)} = \frac{P_1\Delta_1 + P_2\Delta_2}{1 - (L_1 + L_2)}\] \[\frac{Y(s)}{X(s)} = \frac{G_1 + G_2}{1 - (-HG_1 - HG_2)}\] \[\frac{Y(s)}{X(s)} = \frac{G_1 + G_2}{1 + H(G_1 + G_2)}\]
\[\boxed{(C) \ \ \dfrac{G_1+G_2}{1+H(G_1+G_2)}}\]

questions.question: The open loop poles of a third order unity feedback system are at \(0, -1, -2\). Let the frequency corresponding to the point where the root locus of the system transits to unstable region be \(K\). Now suppose we introduce a zero in the open loop transfer function at \(-3\), while keeping all the earlier open loop poles intact. Which one of the following is TRUE about the point where the root locus of the modified system transits to unstable region?
options: It corresponds to a frequency greater than \(K\)
It corresponds to a frequency less than \(K\)
Root locus of modified system never transits to unstable region
questions.explanation:
Case I: Original System \[G(s)H(s) = \frac{K_1}{s(s+1)(s+2)} = \frac{K_1}{s^3 + 3s^2 + 2s}\] The characteristic equation is \(s^3 + 3s^2 + 2s + K_1 = 0\). \[\begin{array}{c|cc} s^3 & 1 & 2 \\ s^2 & 3 & K_1 \\ s^1 & \dfrac{6-K_1}{3} & 0 \\ s^0 & K_1 & 0 \end{array}\] For stability, \(\dfrac{6-K_1}{3} > 0 \implies K_1 < 6\). At \(K_1 = 6\), the system crosses the \(j\omega\)-axis and transits to the unstable region. img/ch5_root_locus/5_15_1_A.png Case II: Modified System (Adding a Zero at \(-3\))
\[G(s)H(s) = \frac{K_1(s+3)}{s(s+1)(s+2)}\] The modified characteristic equation is: \[s^3 + 3s^2 + (2+K_1)s + 3K_1 = 0\] \[\begin{array}{c|cc} s^3 & 1 & 2+K_1 \\ s^2 & 3 & 3K_1 \\ s^1 & 2 \\ s^0 & 3K_1 \end{array}\] No sign changes in the 1st column. Thus, the root locus of the modified system never enters the right-half of the \(s\)-plane. img/ch5_root_locus/5_15_1_B.png \[\boxed{\text{(D) \ Root locus of modified system never transits to unstable region}}\]
Key points
Adding an open-loop zero pulls the root locus branches towards the left-half of the \(s\)-plane (LHP), which generally increases the relative stability of the system.

questions.question: An open loop transfer function \(G(s)\) of a system is \[G(s) = \frac{K}{s(s + 1)(s + 2)}\] For a unity feedback system, the breakaway point of the root loci on the real axis occurs at,
questions.explanation:
Given the open-loop transfer function: \[G(s) = \frac{K}{s(s+1)(s+2)}\] The characteristic equation for the unity feedback system is: \[1 + G(s) = 0\] \[s(s^2 + 3s + 2) + K = 0\] \[-K = s^3 + 3s^2 + 2s\] Differentiating both sides with respect to \(s\) to find the breakaway points: \[\frac{dK}{ds} = 0 \implies 3s^2 + 6s + 2 = 0\] Solving the quadratic equation: \[s = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 24}}{6} = -1 \pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\] \[s = -0.42 \quad \text{or} \quad s = -1.58\] \(s = -0.42\) lies between \(0\) and \(-1\), so it is a valid breakaway point where \(K > 0\). \(s = -1.58\) does not lie on the root locus, corresponding to a negative value of \(K\). \[\boxed{(A) \ \ -0.42}\]
Key points
Valid breakaway points must satisfy \(\frac{dK}{ds} = 0\) and exist on the root locus path.

questions.ref: Polar Plot and Frequency Response of Second Order Systems Q1
questions.question: The transfer function of a second order real system with a perfectly flat magnitude response of unity has a pole at \((2-j3)\). List all the poles and zeroes.
options: Poles at \((\pm2-j3)\), one zero at origin.
Poles at \((2\pm j3)\), zeroes at \((-2\pm j3)\).
questions.explanation:
Since the system is a second-order real system and has a pole at \(s=2-j3\), its complex conjugate must also be a pole. Hence, the poles are \[s=2\pm j3\] A perfectly flat magnitude response of unity implies that \[|G(j\omega)|=1,\qquad \forall\,\omega\] Therefore, the system is an all-pass system. For a continuous-time all-pass system, every pole at \(s=p\) has a corresponding zero at \(s=-p^{*}\). Hence, corresponding to the poles at \(s=2\pm j3,\) the zeros are located at \[s=-2\pm j3\] Therefore, \[\boxed{\text{(D) Poles at }(2\pm j3),\ \text{zeros at }(-2\pm j3)}\]
Key points
  • A real system must have complex poles and zeros in conjugate pairs.
  • In a continuous-time all-pass system, zeros are obtained by reflecting the poles about the imaginary axis.

questions.question: Nyquist plots of two functions \(G_1(s)\) and \(G_2(s)\) are shown in figure. Nyquist plot of the product of \(G_1(s)\) and \(G_2(s)\) is
questions.explanation:
From the given Nyquist plots, img/ch7_nyquist_plot/7_15_1_1.png Since the locus lies entirely on the negative imaginary axis, \[G_1(j\omega)=K_1e^{-j90^\circ} =-jK_1, \qquad K_1 > 0\] img/ch7_nyquist_plot/7_15_1_2.png Since the locus lies entirely on the positive imaginary axis, \[G_2(j\omega)=K_2e^{j90^\circ} =jK_2, \qquad K_2 > 0\] Therefore, \[G_1(j\omega)G_2(j\omega) = (-jK_1)(jK_2) = K_1K_2\] Since \(K_1 > 0\) and \(K_2 > 0\), \[G_1(j\omega)G_2(j\omega) > 0\] Hence, the Nyquist plot of the product is a constant with phase \(0^\circ\). Therefore, the correct Nyquist plot is option (B). \[\boxed{(B)}\]

  • Any point on the negative real axis can be represented as \(-K\), where \(K > 0\).
  • Any point on the positive imaginary axis can be represented as \(jK\), where \(K > 0\).
  • Any point on the negative imaginary axis can be represented as \(-jK\), where \(K > 0\).
  • Here, \(K\) denotes the magnitude (distance from the origin) and is not necessarily a constant gain.

questions.question: Two semi-infinite conducting sheets are placed at right angles to each other as shown in the figure. A point charge of \(+Q\) is placed at a distance of \(d\) from both sheets. The net force on the charge is \(\dfrac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\dfrac{K}{d^2}\), where \(K\) is given by [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] By the image charge method, the charge configuration is replaced by suitable image charges and the force on charge \(Q\) is obtained by superposition. The force components are \[\vec{F}_{14} = \frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(2d)^2} (-\hat{y})\] \[\vec{F}_{12} = \frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(2d)^2} (-\hat{x})\] The diagonal image charge is at a distance \[2\sqrt{2}\,d\] Hence, \[\vec{F}_{13} = \frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(2\sqrt{2}d)^2} \left( \frac{\hat{x}}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{\hat{y}}{\sqrt{2}} \right)\] The net force is \[\vec{F}_1 = \vec{F}_{12} + \vec{F}_{13} + \vec{F}_{14}\] \[\vec{F}_1 = \frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0d^2} \left[ \left( \frac{1}{8\sqrt{2}} -\frac{1}{4} \right)\hat{x} + \left( \frac{1}{8\sqrt{2}} -\frac{1}{4} \right)\hat{y} \right]\] Let \[\vec{F}_1 = \frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0d^2}\,\vec{K}\] Therefore, \[\vec{K} = \left( \frac{1}{8\sqrt{2}} -\frac{1}{4} \right)\hat{x} + \left( \frac{1}{8\sqrt{2}} -\frac{1}{4} \right)\hat{y}\] \[\vec{K} = \frac{1-2\sqrt{2}}{8\sqrt{2}}\hat{x} + \frac{1-2\sqrt{2}}{8\sqrt{2}}\hat{y}\] \[\vec{K} = \frac{1-2\sqrt{2}}{8\sqrt{2}}\hat{i} + \frac{1-2\sqrt{2}}{8\sqrt{2}}\hat{j}\] Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{D}}\]
Key points
  • Image charge method replaces conducting boundaries with equivalent image charges.
  • Net force is obtained by vector addition of forces due to all image charges.
  • Coulomb force magnitude is inversely proportional to the square of separation distance.
  • Diagonal image charge contributes equally along \(\hat{x}\) and \(\hat{y}\) directions.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not forget that the diagonal image charge is located at a distance \(2\sqrt{2}\,d\).
  • Resolve the diagonal force into \(\hat{x}\) and \(\hat{y}\) components using \(1/\sqrt{2}\).
  • Maintain proper signs while adding vector components.
  • Do not add force magnitudes directly; perform vector addition.

questions.question: A parallel plate capacitor is partially filled with glass of dielectric constant \(4.0\) as shown below. The dielectric strength of air and glass are \(30\,\text{kV/cm}\) and \(300\,\text{kV/cm}\), respectively. The maximum voltage (in kilovolts) which can be applied across the capacitor without any breakdown is [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Capacitance of the air capacitor is \[C_{\text{air}} = (\varepsilon_0\times1)\frac{A}{5\,\text{mm}} = C_1\] Capacitance of the glass capacitor is \[C_{\text{glass}} = (\varepsilon_0\times4)\frac{A}{5\,\text{mm}} = 4C_1\] If air reaches its dielectric strength of \(30\,\text{kV/cm}\), the maximum voltage across the air layer is \[V_a = 30\times0.5 = 15\,\text{kV}\] Since \[X_C\propto\frac{1}{C},\] the glass capacitor has one-fourth the reactance of the air capacitor. Hence, \[V_g = \frac{V_a}{4} = \frac{15}{4} = 3.75\,\text{kV}\] Therefore, the total applied voltage is \[V = V_a+V_g = 15+3.75 = 18.75\,\text{kV}\] Although the dielectric strength of glass is \(300\,\text{kV/cm}\), the air layer reaches its breakdown limit first. Therefore, dielectric breakdown occurs in the air before the glass reaches its breakdown voltage. Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{18.75}\]
Key points
  • Parallel-plate capacitance: \[C=\varepsilon\frac{A}{d}.\]
  • For capacitors in series, voltage divides inversely proportional to capacitance.
  • Breakdown occurs first in the dielectric having the lower withstand voltage.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume equal voltage across dielectric layers connected in series.
  • Do not compare only dielectric strengths; compare the actual voltage across each dielectric.
  • Remember that the dielectric with larger capacitance has the smaller voltage drop.

questions.question: A steady current \(I\) is flowing in the \(-x\) direction through each of two infinitely long wires at \(y=\pm \dfrac{L}{2}\) as shown in the figure. The permeability of the medium is \(\mu_0\). The \(\vec{B}\)-field at \((0,L,0)\) is [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] The direction of current in both wires is along the \(-\hat{x}\) direction. Using the right-hand thumb rule, the magnetic field at the point \((0,L,0)\) due to both wires is in the \(-\hat{z}\) direction. By Ampere's circuital law, for a long straight conductor, \[\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I\] For wire \(1\), the distance from \((0,L,0)\) is \[r_1=\frac{L}{2}\] Hence, \[B_1(2\pi r_1) = \mu_0 I\] \[B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{\pi L}\] For wire \(2\), the distance from \((0,L,0)\) is \[r_2=\frac{3L}{2}\] Therefore, \[B_2(2\pi r_2) = \mu_0 I\] \[B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi\left(\frac{3L}{2}\right)} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{3\pi L}\] Since both magnetic fields are directed along \(-\hat{z}\), they add directly. \[\vec{B}(0,L,0) = -(B_1+B_2)\hat{z}\] \[\vec{B}(0,L,0) = -\left( \frac{\mu_0 I}{\pi L} + \frac{\mu_0 I}{3\pi L} \right)\hat{z}\] \[\vec{B}(0,L,0) = -\frac{\mu_0 I}{\pi L} \left(1+\frac{1}{3}\right)\hat{z}\] \[\vec{B}(0,L,0) = -\frac{4\mu_0 I}{3\pi L}\hat{z}\] Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{A}\]
Key points
  • Magnetic field due to a long straight current-carrying conductor is \[B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}.\]
  • The direction of magnetic field is determined using the right-hand thumb rule.
  • Magnetic fields are vector quantities and must be added vectorially.
  • Ampere's circuital law for a straight conductor is \[\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l}=\mu_0 I.\]

questions.question: A separately excited DC generator has an armature resistance of \(0.1\,\Omega\) and negligible armature inductance. At rated field current and rated rotor speed, its open-circuit voltage is \(200\,\text{V}\). When this generator is operated at half the rated speed, with half the rated field current, an uncharged \(1000\,\mu\text{F}\) capacitor is suddenly connected across the armature terminals. Assume that the speed remains unchanged during the transient. At what time (in microsecond) after the capacitor is connected will the voltage across it reach \(25\,\text{V}\)?
questions.explanation:
Induced emf in a DC generator is given by \[E_{g}=\frac{\phi NZ}{60}\left(\frac{P}{A}\right)\] Hence, \[E_{g}\propto \phi N\] Therefore, \[\frac{E_{g2}}{E_{g1}}=\frac{\phi_{2}N_{2}}{\phi_{1}N_{1}}\] Since field current and speed are halved, \[\frac{\phi_{2}}{\phi_{1}}=0.5 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}=0.5\] \[\frac{E_{g2}}{E_{g1}}=0.5\times0.5=0.25\] \[E_{g2}=200\times0.25=50\,\text{V}\] For charging RC circuit, [figure unavailable] \[V_{c}=E_{g}\left(1-e^{-t/RC}\right)\] \[25=50\left(1-e^{-t/RC}\right)\] \[e^{-t/RC}=0.5\] \[t=-RC\ln(0.5)\] \[t=69.3\,\mu\text{sec}\] \[\boxed{B}\]
Key points
  • Generated emf of a DC generator is proportional to flux and speed, i.e., \(E_{g}\propto \phi N\).
  • In an RC charging circuit, capacitor voltage is given by \(V_{c}=E_{g}\left(1-e^{-t/RC}\right)\).
  • Halving both flux and speed reduces generated emf to one-fourth of its original value.
  • Time constant of RC circuit is \(\tau=RC\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not forget that both flux and speed are halved; emf becomes \(0.25\) times, not \(0.5\) times.
  • Do not use discharging capacitor equation in place of charging equation.
  • Ensure natural logarithm \(\ln\) is used while solving exponential equations.
  • Be careful with unit conversion; final answer is in \(\mu\text{sec}\).

questions.question: A separately excited DC motor runs at \(1000\,\text{rpm}\) on no load when its armature terminals are connected to a \(200\,\text{V}\) DC source and the rated voltage is applied to the field winding. The armature resistance of this motor is \(1\,\Omega\). The no-load armature current is negligible. With the motor developing its full load torque, the armature voltage is set so that the rotor speed is \(500\,\text{rpm}\). When the load torque is reduced to \(50\%\) of the full load value under the same armature voltage conditions, the speed rises to \(520\,\text{rpm}\). Neglecting the rotational losses, the full load armature current (in Ampere) is .
questions.explanation:
Under no load, \[I_{a}=0\] Therefore, \[V_{t}=E_{b}\] \[E_{b1}=200\,\text{V} \quad \text{at} \quad N_{1}=1000\,\text{rpm}\] Since the motor is separately excited, flux can be assumed constant. \[E_{b}\propto N\] \[\frac{E_{b2}}{E_{b1}}=\frac{N_{2}}{N_{1}}=\frac{500}{1000}\] \[E_{b2}=100\,\text{V}\] For rated torque, let armature current be \(I_{a}\). Since \(\phi\) is constant, \[T\propto I_{a}\] At half rated torque, \[I_{a2}=\frac{I_{a}}{2}\] At \(N_{3}=520\,\text{rpm}\), \[\frac{E_{b3}}{E_{b1}}=\frac{N_{3}}{N_{1}}=\frac{520}{1000}\] \[E_{b3}=104\,\text{V}\] Using voltage equation, \[V_{t}=E_{b2}+I_{a}R_{a}\] \[V_{t}=E_{b3}+\frac{I_{a}}{2}R_{a}\] Substituting values, \[100+I_{a}R_{a}=104+\frac{I_{a}}{2}R_{a}\] \[4=\frac{I_{a}}{2}R_{a}\] \[I_{a}=\frac{8}{R_{a}}\] Given \(R_{a}=1\,\Omega\), \[I_{a}=8\,\text{A}\] Therefore, full load armature current is \[\boxed{8}\]
Key points
  • For separately excited DC motors, flux \(\phi\) remains constant.
  • Back emf is directly proportional to speed, i.e., \(E_{b}\propto N\).
  • Torque in a separately excited motor is proportional to armature current, i.e., \(T\propto I_{a}\).
  • Motor voltage equation is \(V_{t}=E_{b}+I_{a}R_{a}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume varying flux in separately excited motors unless specified.
  • Do not forget that half torque implies half armature current when flux is constant.
  • Be careful while applying proportionality between back emf and speed.
  • Ensure correct substitution in voltage equations before simplifying.

questions.explanation:
Base load plants are those generating stations which are operated continuously to meet the minimum constant demand of the power system.
  • Wind farms are generally treated as base load plants because once available, they are operated continuously due to negligible fuel cost.
  • Run-of-river hydro plants operate continuously based on river flow and are used as base load plants.
  • Nuclear power plants are highly suitable for base load operation because they operate most efficiently at constant output.
  • Diesel power plants are generally used as peak load or standby plants due to high operating cost.
Hence, the correct statements are: \[\boxed{\text{(C)} \ P,\ Q,\ \text{and}\ R}\]

questions.question: The synchronous generator shown in the figure is supplying active power to an infinite bus via two short, lossless transmission lines, and is initially in steady state. The mechanical power input to the generator and the voltage magnitude \(E\) are constant. If one line is tripped at time \(t_1\) by opening the circuit breakers at the two ends (although there is no fault), then it is seen that the generator undergoes a stable transient. Which one of the following waveforms of the rotor angle \(\delta\) shows the transient correctly?
questions.explanation:
Initially, the synchronous generator operates in steady state with both transmission lines in service. When one transmission line is tripped at time \(t_1\), the transfer reactance between the generator and infinite bus increases. Hence, the maximum power transfer capability \[P_{\max} = \frac{EV}{X}\] decreases. Since the mechanical input power remains unchanged immediately after line tripping, \[P_m > P_e\] Therefore, the rotor accelerates and the rotor angle \(\delta\) increases. As the system is stable, the rotor angle undergoes damped oscillations about the new equilibrium operating point. Thus, the correct waveform is the one in which:
  • rotor angle increases immediately after \(t_1\)
  • oscillations are stable and decaying
  • final operating point is at a higher \(\delta\)
Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{(A)}}\]
Key points
  • Tripping a transmission line increases transfer reactance.
  • Increase in reactance reduces: \[P_{\max} = \frac{EV}{X}\]
  • If mechanical power exceeds electrical power: \[P_m > P_e\] the rotor accelerates and \(\delta\) increases.
  • Stable systems exhibit damped rotor-angle oscillations.

questions.ref: Power System Matrices and Load Flow Q1
questions.question: Determine the correctness or otherwise of the following Assertion [a] and the Reason [r]. Assertion: Fast decoupled load flow method gives approximate load flow solution because it uses several assumptions. Reason: Accuracy depends on the power mismatch vector tolerance.
options: Both [a] and [r] are true and [r] is the correct reason for [a].
Both [a] and [r] are true but [r] is not the correct reason for [a].
questions.explanation:
The Fast Decoupled Load Flow (FDLF) method simplifies the Newton-Raphson load flow equations using assumptions such as:
  • Transmission lines are predominantly reactive.
  • Voltage angle differences are small.
  • Real power is mainly dependent on voltage angle.
  • Reactive power is mainly dependent on voltage magnitude.
These assumptions reduce computational complexity but still provide sufficiently accurate results for practical power systems. Hence, the assertion is true. The reason statement says that accuracy depends on the power mismatch vector tolerance. This statement is also true because convergence accuracy in iterative load flow methods depends on the selected tolerance value. However, this is not the reason why the Fast Decoupled Load Flow method gives an approximate solution. The approximation arises because of the simplifying assumptions used in Jacobian decoupling. Therefore, \[\boxed{\text{(D) [a] is false and [r] is true.}}\]

questions.question: Consider the economic dispatch problem for a power plant having two generating units. The fuel costs in Rs/MWh along with the generation limits for the two units are given below: \[C_1(P_1) = 0.01P_1^2 + 30P_1 + 10\] \[100\,\text{MW} \leq P_1 \leq 150\,\text{MW}\] \[C_2(P_2) = 0.05P_2^2 + 10P_2 + 10\] \[100\,\text{MW} \leq P_2 \leq 180\,\text{MW}\] The incremental cost (in Rs/MWh) of the power plant when it supplies \(200\,\text{MW}\) is .
questions.explanation:
Given, \[C_1(P_1) = 0.01P_1^2 + 30P_1 + 10\] \[100\,\text{MW} \leq P_1 \leq 150\,\text{MW}\] \[C_2(P_2) = 0.05P_2^2 + 10P_2 + 10\] \[100\,\text{MW} \leq P_2 \leq 180\,\text{MW}\] Total load demand is \[P_1 + P_2 = 200\,\text{MW} \tag{1}\] For economic dispatch, \[\frac{dC_1}{dP_1} = \frac{dC_2}{dP_2}\] Differentiating, \[0.02P_1 + 30 = 0.1P_2 + 10\] \[0.1P_2 - 0.02P_1 = 20 \tag{2}\] Solving the economic dispatch equations without considering the generation limits from equations (1) and (2) gives \[P_2=200~\text{MW}, \qquad P_1=0~\text{MW}.\] However, this operating point is not feasible since \[P_2>180~\text{MW},\] which violates the upper generation limit of Generator~2. If Generator~2 is fixed at its maximum permissible output, \[P_2=180~\text{MW},\] then, from the power balance equation, \[P_1=200-180=20~\text{MW}.\] This also violates the operating constraint of Generator~1 because \[P_1<100~\text{MW},\] which is below its minimum permissible generation. Thus, the equal incremental cost solution cannot be achieved while satisfying the generator limits. Since the total load demand is only \(200~\text{MW}\) and both generators have a minimum operating limit of \(100~\text{MW}\), the only feasible generation schedule is \[P_1=100~\text{MW}, \qquad P_2=100~\text{MW}.\] The corresponding incremental cost is evaluated using the cost function of Generator~2, \[\frac{dC_2}{dP_2} = 0.1P_2+10 = 0.1(100)+10 = 20~\text{Rs/MWh}.\] Therefore, the required answer is \[\boxed{20}\]
Key points
  • The unconstrained economic dispatch must always be verified against the generator operating limits.
  • Enforcing one generator limit may cause another generator to violate its own operating limit.
  • When the equal incremental cost criterion is infeasible, the operating point is determined by the active generation constraints.

questions.question: For the switching converter shown in the following figure, assume steady-state operation. Also assume that the components are ideal, the inductor current is always positive and continuous, and the switching period is \(T_s\). If the voltage \(V_L\) is as shown, the duty cycle of the switch \(S\) is . [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
Method 1
[figure unavailable] From the given inductor voltage waveform, we can determine the operation of the converter during different switching intervals. During the interval \(0 \leq t \leq T_{\text{on}}\): \[V_{s} = V_{L} = 15\,\text{V}\] During the interval \(T_{\text{on}} \leq t \leq T\): \[V_{L} = -(V_{0} - V_{s}) = -45\,\text{V}\] Given that the input voltage \(V_{s} = 15\,\text{V}\): \[-(V_{0} - 15) = -45\,\text{V}\] \[V_{0} = 60\,\text{V}\] Hence, it is a boost regulator. The relationship between output and input voltage is given by: \[V_{0} = \left( \frac{1}{1 - \alpha} \right) V_{s}\] Substituting the values: \[60 = \left( \frac{1}{1 - \alpha} \right) 15\] \[1 - \alpha = \frac{15}{60} = 0.25\] \[\alpha = 0.75\]
Method 2
Since the inductor current is always continuous, we can apply the inductor volt-second balance equation over one complete switching period \(T\): \[\int_{0}^{T} V_{L} \, dt = 0\] Let \(D\) be the duty cycle (\(D = \alpha\)). From the waveform: \[15 \cdot DT + (-45) \cdot (1 - D)T = 0\] \[15D = 45(1 - D)\] \[60D = 45\] \[D = \frac{45}{60} = \frac{3}{4} = 0.75\] Therefore, the duty cycle of the regulator is: \[\boxed{0.75}\]
Key points
  • Volt-Second Balance Principle: For an inductor operating in steady-state continuous conduction mode, the net volt-seconds applied to the inductor over a complete switching period must be zero.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure that the negative sign for the inductor voltage during the OFF period is properly accounted for when setting up the volt-second balance equation.

questions.ref: DC to AC Converter- Inverter Q1
questions.question: The single-phase full-bridge voltage source inverter (VSI), shown in figure, has an output frequency of \(50\,\text{Hz}\). It uses unipolar pulse width modulation with switching frequency of \(50\,\text{kHz}\) and modulation index of \(0.7\). For \(V_{in}=100\,\text{V DC}\), \(L=9.55\,\text{mH}\), \(C=63.66\,\mu\text{F}\), and \(R=5\,\Omega\), the amplitude of the fundamental component in the output voltage \(V_o\) (in Volt) under steady-state is . [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
The RMS value of the fundamental component of the output voltage for the Voltage Source Inverter (\(\text{VSI}\)) is given by: \[V_{R1} = \frac{V_s}{\sqrt{2}} \times m_a\] Substituting the given values (\(V_s = 100\,\text{V}\) and \(m_a = 0.7\)): \[V_{R1} = \frac{100}{\sqrt{2}} \times 0.7 = 49.49\,\text{V}\] The amplitude (peak value) of this fundamental component is: \[V_{R\text{peak}} = \sqrt{2} \times 49.49 = 70\,\text{V}\] Here, \(V_{R\text{peak}}\) is the amplitude of the fundamental voltage at the output of the full-bridge \(\text{VSI}\). The parameter \(V_{o(\text{peak})}\) represents the amplitude of the fundamental voltage across the parallel load resistor. First, let's find the capacitive reactance \(X_c\) at the fundamental frequency (\(f = 50\,\text{Hz}\)): \[X_c = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 63.66 \times 10^{-6}} = 50\,\Omega\] The equivalent impedance \(Z\) of the parallel combination of the resistor \(R\) and capacitor \(C\) is: \[Z = \frac{R(-jX_c)}{R - jX_c} = \frac{5(-j50)}{5 - j50} = 4.97\angle -5.71^\circ\,\Omega\] Next, find the inductive reactance \(X_L\) of the filter inductor: \[X_L = \omega L = 2\pi \times 50 \times 9.55 \times 10^{-3} = 3\,\Omega\] Using the voltage divider rule, the peak fundamental output voltage across the load \(V_{o(\text{peak})}\) is: \[V_{o(\text{peak})} = V_{R\text{peak}} \times \frac{Z}{Z + jX_L}\] \[V_{o(\text{peak})} = 70 \times \frac{4.97\angle -5.71^\circ}{(4.97\angle -5.71^\circ) + j3} = 62.75\angle -32.5^\circ\,\text{V}\] Therefore, the amplitude of the fundamental component in the output voltage is: \[V_o = 62.75\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{62.75}\]
Key points
  • The fundamental peak output voltage of a single-phase full-bridge inverter under sinusoidal pulse width modulation (\(\text{SPWM}\)) is directly proportional to the amplitude modulation index \(m_a\) for \(m_a \le 1\).
  • High-frequency harmonics generated by the inverter switching are smoothed out using a low-pass \(\text{LC}\) filter, allowing only the fundamental line frequency component to reach the load safely.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure that the frequency \(\omega = 2\pi f\) uses the fundamental system frequency (\(50\,\text{Hz}\)) instead of the switching frequency of the inverter.

Instrument TypeUsed for

questions.explanation:
P. Permanent Magnet Moving Coil (PMMC)
For PMMC instrument, \[T_d\propto BI\] Torque depends on current direction. For AC, current reverses every half cycle, hence torque also reverses every half cycle. Therefore, \[T_{\text{avg}}=0\] Thus PMMC works only for: \[\boxed{\text{DC only}}\] Hence, \[P\rightarrow1\] Q. Moving iron connected through Current Transformer (CT)
For moving iron instrument, \[T_d\propto I^2\] Hence, \[(+I)^2=(-I)^2\] So MI instrument alone can measure AC and DC. But CT works only on AC because: \[e=N\frac{d\phi}{dt}\] For DC, \[\frac{d\phi}{dt}=0\] Thus, \[\boxed{\text{MI + CT works only on AC}}\] Hence, \[Q\rightarrow2\] R. Rectifier instrument
A rectifier instrument uses: \[\text{AC/DC}\rightarrow\text{Rectifier}\rightarrow\text{PMMC}\] Rectifier converts AC into DC before feeding PMMC. Thus it can measure: \[\boxed{\text{AC and DC}}\] Hence, \[R\rightarrow3\] S. Electrodynamometer
For electrodynamometer, \[T_d\propto I_1I_2\] For AC, \[(-I_1)(-I_2)=I_1I_2\] Hence torque remains positive for both AC and DC. Therefore, \[\boxed{\text{AC and DC}}\] Hence, \[S\rightarrow3\] Final matching: \[P\rightarrow1,\quad Q\rightarrow2,\quad R\rightarrow3,\quad S\rightarrow3\] Therefore, the correct option is \[\boxed{\textbf{C. }\text{P-1, Q-2, R-3, S-3}}\]

questions.subject: measurements
questions.question: A 3-phase balanced load which has a power factor of \(0.707\) is connected to a balanced supply. The power consumed by the load is \(5\,\text{kW}\). The power is measured by the two-wattmeter method. The readings of the two wattmeters are
questions.explanation:
Given:
\[P=5\,\text{kW},\qquad \text{PF}=0.707\Rightarrow \cos\phi=0.707\Rightarrow \phi=45^\circ\]
Method 1
For two-wattmeter method, \[W_1+W_2=P=5\] and \[\tan\phi=\sqrt{3}\,\frac{W_1-W_2}{W_1+W_2}\] Substituting \(\phi=45^\circ\), \[1=\sqrt{3}\,\frac{W_1-W_2}{5} \Rightarrow W_1-W_2=\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}=2.887\] Now, \[W_1+W_2=5,\qquad W_1-W_2=2.887\] \[2W_1=7.887\Rightarrow W_1=3.944\,\text{kW}\] \[W_2=5-3.944=1.056\,\text{kW}\]
Method 2
For a balanced load, \[W_1=V_LI_L\cos(30^\circ+\phi),\qquad W_2=V_LI_L\cos(30^\circ-\phi)\] With \(\phi=45^\circ\), \[W_1:W_2=\cos75^\circ:\cos15^\circ=0.2588:0.9659=1:3.732\] Also, \[W_1+W_2=5\] Let \(W_1=x\), then \(W_2=3.732x\). So, \[x+3.732x=5\Rightarrow x=1.056\] \[W_1=1.056\,\text{kW},\qquad W_2=3.944\,\text{kW}\]
\[\boxed{\textbf{A. }\text{3.94 kW and 1.06 kW}}\]

questions.subject: measurements
questions.question: The coils of a wattmeter have resistances \(0.01\,\Omega\) and \(1000\,\Omega\); their inductances may be neglected. The wattmeter is connected as shown in the figure, to measure the power consumed by a load, which draws \(25\,\text{A}\) at power factor \(0.8\). The voltage across the load terminals is \(30\,\text{V}\). The percentage error on the wattmeter reading is . [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] From the figure, the current coil (CC) is in series with the load and the pressure coil (PC) is connected across the load only. Therefore, the wattmeter measures \[P_m=P_{\text{load}}+P_{\text{PC}}\] True load power:
\[P_{\text{true}}=VI\cos\phi=30\times25\times0.8=600\,\text{W}\] Pressure coil power loss:
\[P_{\text{PC}}=\frac{V^2}{R_P}=\frac{30^2}{1000}=0.9\,\text{W}\] Hence, \[P_m=600+0.9=600.9\,\text{W}\] Percentage error:
\[\%\text{ error} = \frac{600.9-600}{600}\times100 = 0.15\%\] \[\boxed{0.15}\]

questions.subject: measurements
questions.question: An unbalanced DC Wheatstone bridge is shown in the figure. At what value of \(p\) will the magnitude of \(V_0\) be maximum? [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] Need to maximize: \[|V_0|=|V_A-V_B|\] Supply voltage = E Step 1: Find node voltage \(V_A\) Using voltage division in the right branch: Upper resistance = pR Lower resistance = R(1+x) Hence, \[V_A = E\frac{R(1+x)}{pR+R(1+x)} = E\frac{1+x}{p+1+x}\] Step 2: Find node voltage \(V_B\) Similarly for the left branch: Upper resistance = pR Lower resistance = R Thus, \[V_B = E\frac{R}{pR+R} = E\frac{1}{p+1}\] Step 3: Find bridge output voltage
\[V_0=V_A-V_B\] Substituting, \[V_0 = E\left( \frac{1+x}{p+1+x} - \frac{1}{p+1} \right)\] Taking LCM, \[V_0 = E \frac{ (1+x)(p+1)-(p+1+x) } { (p+1)(p+1+x) }\] Simplifying numerator, \[(1+x)(p+1)-(p+1+x) = px\] Hence, \[V_0 = E \frac{px}{(p+1)(p+1+x)}\] Since \(E\) and \(x\) are constants, maximize: \[f(p)=\frac{p}{(p+1)(p+1+x)}\] Step 4: Differentiate
\[f(p)=\frac{p}{p^2+p(2+x)+(1+x)}\] Using quotient rule, \[f'(p) = \frac{ [p^2+p(2+x)+(1+x)]-p(2p+2+x) } { [p^2+p(2+x)+(1+x)]^2 }\] For maximum value: \[f'(p)=0\] Thus, \[p^2+p(2+x)+(1+x)=p(2p+2+x)\] Simplifying, \[1+x=p^2\] Therefore, \[\boxed{ \textbf{A. }\sqrt{1+x} }\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Read the following paragraph and choose the correct statement. Climate change has reduced human security and threatened human well being. An ignored reality of human progress is that human security largely depends upon environmental security. But on the contrary, human progress seems contradictory to environmental security. To keep up both at the required level is a challenge to be addressed by one and all. One of the ways to curb the climate change may be suitable scientific innovations, while the other may be the Gandhian perspective on small scale progress with focus on sustainability.
options: Human progress and security are positively associated with environmental security.
Human progress is contradictory to environmental security.
Human security is contradictory to environmental security.
Human progress depends upon environmental security.
questions.explanation:
Based on the provided passage, let us analyze the relationships described:
  • The text mentions an ignored reality: "human security largely depends upon environmental security."
  • However, it immediately introduces a contrasting reality about progress: "But on the contrary, human progress seems contradictory to environmental security."
Let us evaluate the choices against these statements:
  • Option A: Incorrect. Human progress is explicitly stated to be contradictory, not positively associated.
  • Option B: Correct. This directly echoes the literal sentence from the passage: "human progress seems contradictory to environmental security."
  • Option C: Incorrect. The passage states human security depends upon environmental security, not that it is contradictory to it.
  • Option D: Incorrect. The passage states that human security (not human progress) depends upon environmental security.
\[\boxed{\text{B) Human progress is contradictory to environmental security.}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Humpty Dumpty sits on a wall every day while having lunch. The wall sometimes breaks. A person sitting on the wall falls if the wall breaks. Which one of the statements below is logically valid and can be inferred from the above sentences?
options: Humpty Dumpty always falls while having lunch
Humpty Dumpty does not fall sometimes while having lunch
Humpty Dumpty never falls during dinner
When Humpty Dumpty does not sit on the wall, the wall does not break
questions.explanation:
Let us evaluate the statements step by step based on strict logical constraints provided in the premise:
  • Premise 1: Humpty Dumpty sits on a wall every day while having lunch.
  • Premise 2: The wall sometimes breaks.
  • Premise 3: A person sitting on the wall falls if the wall breaks (\(\text{Wall breaks} \rightarrow \text{Person falls}\)).
Let us analyze the logical validity of each choice:
  • Option A: Incorrect. Because the wall only breaks sometimes, Humpty Dumpty will only fall on the days when the wall breaks. He does not fall always.
  • Option B: Correct. Since the wall breaks only sometimes, it implies that on the remaining days, the wall does not break. If the wall does not break, Humpty Dumpty does not fall on those specific days. Thus, he does not fall sometimes while having lunch.
  • Option C: Incorrect. The passage provides zero information regarding what happens during dinner.
  • Option D: Incorrect. This assumes an inverse relationship (\(\neg \text{Condition} \rightarrow \neg \text{Consequence}\)). The premise states that if a person sits on it and it breaks, they fall, but it does not claim that a person sitting on it is the single cause behind the wall breaking.
\[\boxed{\text{B)Humpty Dumpty does not fall sometimes while having lunch}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Given below are two statements followed by two conclusions. Assuming these statements to be true, decide which one logically follows. Statements:
  • I. All film stars are playback singers.
  • II. All film directors are film stars.
Conclusions:
  • I. All film directors are playback singers.
  • II. Some film stars are film directors.
options: Neither conclusion I nor II follows.
Both conclusions I and II follow.
questions.explanation:
Statements:
  1. All film stars are playback singers.
  2. All film directors are film stars.
From I and II: All film directors are film stars (II), and all film stars are playback singers (I), so: \[\text{Film directors} \subset \text{Film stars} \subset \text{Playback singers}\] Conclusion I: All film directors are playback singers — TRUE (transitive). \(\checkmark\) Conclusion II: Some film stars are film directors — TRUE (since all film directors are film stars, film directors form a subset of film stars). \(\checkmark\) \[\boxed{\text{D) Both conclusions I and II follow}}\]
Key points
  • Transitivity: If \(A \subset B\) and \(B \subset C\), then \(A \subset C\).
  • If all A are B, then some B are A (conversion of universal affirmative).
